The non-parametric memory in the RAG models described in the paper is the retrieval component that allows the model to access external information without updating its weights. Specifically, the RAG model uses a retriever to fetch relevant text documents based on the input query, which are then used as additional context during the generation process. [3][4]

The authors partnered with HuggingFace to open-source the code for their models. This can be inferred from the following sentence in [3]: "Code to run experiments with RAG has been open-sourced as part of the HuggingFace Transformers Library [66] and can be found at https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/master/" [3]

The retrieval component \( p_\eta(z|x) \) in RAG follows a bi-encoder architecture, similar to DPR [3]. Specifically, it is defined as:

\[ p_\eta(z|x) \propto \exp \left( d(z)^{\top} q(x) \right) \]

where \( d(z) \) is a dense representation of a document produced by a BERT document encoder, and \( q(x) \) is a query representation produced by a query encoder, both based on BERT. Calculating the top-k documents \( z \) with the highest prior probability \( p_\eta(z|x) \) is a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem, which can be approximately solved in sub-linear time [3].
Each Wikipedia article was split into disjoint 100-word chunks, resulting in a total of 21 million documents. [2]
The dataset used for the fact verification results shown in Table 2 is FEVER [2, 3].

RAG's non-parametric memory is embodied in its retriever component, specifically the Dense Passage Retriever (DPR), which provides latent documents conditioned on the input. The seq2seq model (BART) then conditions on these latent documents along with the input to generate the output. [3]

This non-parametric component helps guide the generation process by drawing on specific knowledge stored in the parametric memory. [2]
The RAG code was open-sourced by HuggingFace [1].

The retrieval component \( p(z|x) \) of RAG is based on DPR and follows a bi-encoder architecture. Specifically, it uses a dense representation \( d(z) \) of a document produced by a BERT document encoder, and a query representation \( q(x) \) produced by a BERT query encoder. The probability of a document \( z \) given a query \( x \) is approximated as:

\[ p(z|x) \propto \exp \left( d(z)^{\top} q(x) \right) \]

Where \( d(z) = BERT(z) \) and \( q(x) = BERT(x) \). Calculating the top-k documents with the highest prior probability involves solving a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem, which can be approximately solved in sub-linear time. [4]

The magnitude of the decrease in adjustable weights when using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) versus training the entire model can be significant. Specifically, the number of trainable parameters for LoRA is given by \(|Θ| = 2 \times Lˆ \times d \times r\), where \(Lˆ\) is the number of weight matrices we apply LoRA to, \(d\) is the dimensionality of the weight matrices, and \(r\) is the rank of the low-rank decomposition matrices. In contrast, training the entire model would involve adjusting all the original parameters, which is much larger, especially for very large models like GPT-3 175B, which has 175 billion trainable parameters.
